steps.speaker: teacher
steps.text: Hello! Today we are exploring equivalent fractions. That means different names for the same amount. Ready, Maisie? Let's go!

steps.speaker: kid
steps.text: Miss Sonia, I've got a chocolate bar cut into two equal parts, and I'm keeping one. That's one half!

steps.speaker: teacher
steps.text: Lovely. Now watch closely. I snap every piece in two, so the bar is cut into quarters. Did your amount of chocolate change?

steps.speaker: kid
steps.text: No! I have two pieces now instead of one, but it is exactly the same amount of chocolate.

steps.speaker: teacher
steps.text: Exactly. One half and two quarters are the same amount, so we call them equivalent fractions. Equivalent simply means same value.

steps.speaker: teacher
steps.text: Quick reminder before the magic trick. The bottom number is the denominator. It tells us how many equal parts the whole is cut into.

steps.speaker: kid
steps.text: And the top number is the numerator. It counts how many of those parts we take!

steps.speaker: teacher
steps.text: Here is the golden rule. Multiply the top AND the bottom by the same number. Two thirds, times two on top and times two on the bottom, becomes four sixths.

steps.speaker: kid
steps.text: I see it in the bars! The pieces get smaller, but we take more of them, so it is still the same amount.

steps.speaker: teacher
steps.text: Why must it be the same number? Because times four on top and times four on the bottom is really multiplying by four quarters. And four quarters is one whole! Multiplying by one changes nothing.

steps.speaker: teacher
steps.text: It works backwards too. Divide top and bottom by the same number to simplify. Twelve eighteenths, divided by six on top and bottom, is two thirds.

steps.speaker: kid
steps.text: Smallest possible numbers, same amount. That is called the simplest form!

steps.speaker: teacher
steps.text: Here is my favourite proof. On the number line, one half and two quarters sit at exactly the same spot. Equivalent fractions always share one spot.

steps.speaker: teacher
steps.text: Your turn, Maisie. Three fifths equals how many twentieths?

steps.speaker: kid
steps.text: The bottom went from five to twenty, that is times four. So the top is three times four. Twelve! Three fifths equals twelve twentieths.

steps.speaker: teacher
steps.text: One more challenge. Are three quarters and nine twelfths equivalent? Look at the bars and decide.

steps.speaker: kid
steps.text: Times three on top, times three on the bottom. Yes, they are equivalent! And the bars shade to exactly the same length.

steps.speaker: teacher
steps.text: Brilliant work! Remember the golden rule. Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number, and the amount never changes. Now off you go and practise!
